title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 8 close: Augustine — multitude of reject shows justice; Epist. 190
pass_a_gloss: Finally, why God who could [save] all, yet has willed to predestine few to life before the multitude of the rejected, two reasons are brought by Augustine, so that there is least need to take refuge in foresight of good and bad works. Thus therefore he: God willed this, that by the very multitude of the rejected it might be shown how of no moment is, with the just God, any number however great of those most justly damned: And that he might persuade that from this those who are redeemed from that very damnation may understand that this was due to that universal mass, which they would see rendered to so great a part of it, Epistle 190.
pass_b_english: Finally: why God, who could save all, yet willed to predestine few to life against the multitude of the rejected — Augustine gives two reasons, so there is little need to take refuge in foresight of good and bad works. Thus he: God willed this, that by the very multitude of the rejected it might be shown how little moment any number of those most justly damned has with the just God — and that those redeemed from that damnation might understand from this that what they see rendered to so great a part of it was due to that universal mass (Epist. 190).
source_text: Postremo, cur Deus qui posset omnes, paucos tamen prae multitudine rejectorum voluerit ad vitam praedestinare, duae rationes ab Augustino afferuntur, ut minime opus sit ad praescientiam bonorum et malorum operum confugere. Sic igitur ille, Hoc voluit Deus, ut ipsa rejectorum multitudine ostenderetur, quam nullius momenti sit apud Deum justum quantalibet numerositas justissime damnatorum: Atque ut suaderet ut hinc intelligant qui ex ipsa damnatione redimuntur, hoc fuisse debitum massae illi universae, quod tam magnae parti ejus redditum cernerent, Epist. 190.
